name: Mercury NZ Limited
overview: Mercury NZ is a New Zealand-listed 'gentailer' — a vertically integrated electricity generator and retailer whose generation fleet is 100% renewable, comprising nine Waikato River hydro stations, five central North Island geothermal stations, and a wind fleet substantially enlarged by the 2021/22 Tilt Renewables acquisition. On the retail side it sells electricity, gas, broadband and mobile services to ~906,000 customer connections under the Mercury, GLOBUG and (post-2022) Trustpower-derived brands. The New Zealand Crown owns 51% of Mercury under the mixed-ownership model (MOM), with the balance free-floating on the NZX (primary) and ASX (foreign-exempt secondary listing); note that Mercury's FY2026 annual result (year ended 30 June 2026) had not yet been reported as of this analysis date (13 August 2026) — the FY2025 result (19 Aug 2025) and the H1 FY2026 result (24 Feb 2026) are the latest hard numbers used below.

business_model.summary: Mercury is a 'gentailer' that earns a wholesale trading margin on electricity it generates and sells into the NZ spot/futures/PPA market, plus a retail margin on electricity, gas, broadband and mobile it on-sells to end customers who it purchases wholesale power for (largely internally hedged). The generation and retail books act as a natural hedge for each other: when spot prices spike, wholesale/trading margin benefits even as retail supply costs rise, and vice versa in low-price periods. Revenue is a mix of largely non-discretionary, recurring retail consumption billing and wholesale/trading revenue that is directly exposed to hydrology and spot-price volatility.

revenue_streams.name: Electricity retail sales to customers
revenue_streams.trend: stable/growing with price increases and connections

revenue_streams.name: Other (carbon units, JV income, management fees)

business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market residential and SME (majority), plus B2B Commercial & Industrial (C&I) customers (e.g. NZ Aluminium Smelters/Tiwai, Fonterra, Visy) and wholesale market counterparties
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand — generation assets in the Waikato (hydro), central North Island/Taupō (geothermal), and Manawatū, South Taranaki, Otago and Southland (wind); retail customers nationwide

main_competitors: Independent retailers (Electric Kiwi, Flick, Frank, Octopus NZ)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'big four' gentailers that together generate roughly 85-90% of New Zealand's electricity and hold ~85% of retail mass-market customers. Mercury holds roughly 19% generation market share and ~16% of GWh sold, making it broadly the third or fourth largest of the four by generation volume behind Meridian (NZ's largest, 100% renewable, hydro/wind-heavy) and roughly comparable in scale to Contact (~80-85% renewable, still has some geothermal/gas peaking) and Genesis (still runs Huntly coal/gas thermal peaking plant and has the lowest renewable share of the four).

moat_factors.description: The Waikato hydro scheme (built 1924-1970) and geothermal fields sit on resource consents and river-control/dam infrastructure that would be extremely difficult and slow to replicate; geothermal in particular gives Mercury a source of 24/7 renewable baseload that intermittent-only generators (pure wind/solar) cannot match.

Owning both generation and retail smooths earnings across hydrology cycles versus a pure generator or pure retailer, and gives Mercury information and pricing advantages regulators are now specifically trying to neutralise (see regulatory risk).
BBB+/Stable S&P rating and Crown-anchored ownership support access to debt markets for a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar renewables build that smaller/independent developers cannot self-fund.

906k connections with 38% of customers on two or more products (power, gas, broadband, mobile) raises switching costs modestly, though NZ retail electricity switching remains relatively easy and price-driven.

Consented/near-consented pipeline >8TWh targeted by 2030 (Kaiwaikawe, Kaiwera Downs II, Ngā Tamariki OEC5, further hydro uprates, fast-track-listed wind projects) gives multi-year visibility competitors must match or cede share.

weaknesses: Hydro output is structurally weather-dependent — FY25 hydro generation was the 4th lowest for the Waikato scheme since 1980 (12th percentile inflows), directly denting both volume and margin

51% Crown ownership caps free float, constrains capital-raising flexibility (MOM rules require the Crown to stay at ≥51%) and makes the company a lightning rod for political intervention on pricing/affordability
Reputational exposure as one of the 'big four' being blamed publicly for winter 2024/2025 supply tightness and high prices, actively 'rebuilding confidence' per FY25 management commentary
Heavy multi-year capex programme is diluting free cash flow and pushing gearing up the target range just as the company also needs to fund a rising dividend

growth_drivers: 3.5TWh of new renewable generation targeted by 2030 (vs. current total generation of ~7.9TWh in FY25), roughly a 44% volume uplift over the decade

Development pipeline to grow beyond 8TWh by 2030, spanning wind (Kaiwaikawe, Kaiwera Downs II, Mahinerangi II, Waikokowai, Puketoi, Tararua repower), geothermal (Ngā Tamariki OEC5, further post-2030 fields) and a major hydro refurbishment programme (~$550m to lift capacity 58MW / generation 87GWh across Maraetai, Ōhakuri and Ātiamuri)
OEC5 (Ngā Tamariki Unit 5) geothermal expansion commissioned/officially opened ~January-March 2026, adding 46MW and ~390GWh/yr of 24/7 renewable baseload just ahead of winter 2026
FY30 EBITDAF target of $1.15-1.25 billion, up from FY26 guidance of $1.0 billion — implies ~15-25% earnings growth over four years if delivered

Electrification/decarbonisation demand growth: long-term supply contracts signed with NZ Aluminium Smelters (Tiwai continuation), Fonterra (Edgecumbe/Waitoa electrification) and Visy; management targets 400GWh of C&I electrification/new demand by 2027
Mercury/Trustpower retail integration synergies: $34m delivered by end-FY25 against an original $35m target, with a further $5m expected in FY26 (target likely to be exceeded)
Grid-scale battery and flexibility development (Whakamaru battery resource consent granted; 50MW of demand-side flexibility targeted for 2026) to help monetise price volatility and support firming
AI/technology-driven optimisation of the Waikato hydro scheme ('Digital River') to extract more value from existing assets without new capex

business.description: Two consecutive years (FY24, FY25) of below-average Waikato/Taupō inflows have directly cut generation volumes and, combined with tight gas supply, driven elevated spot prices that hurt Mercury's 'short' retail position in periods when it is a net buyer. This is the single largest swing factor in reported earnings and cannot be hedged away entirely.

NZ retail electricity is a mature, largely commoditised market with active independent retailers (Electric Kiwi, Flick, Octopus) and easy switching; April 2025 price increases (~9.7% average, mostly pass-through of regulated lines/transmission costs) create headline optics risk even though margin capture is limited.

business.risk: Construction/execution risk on the build programme
business.description: Three major projects (Ngā Tamariki OEC5, Kaiwera Downs II, Kaiwaikawe) running simultaneously exposes Mercury to cost overruns, schedule slippage, supply-chain and skilled-labour shortages (management flags this explicitly), and geopolitical/tariff-driven input cost inflation.

Waikato hydro stations built 1924-1970 require an ongoing multi-hundred-million-dollar refurbishment programme (Karāpiro, Arapuni, Maraetai, Ōhakuri, Ātiamuri) simply to maintain output and safety compliance, competing for capital with growth projects.

financial.risk: Rising gearing through the capex cycle
financial.description: S&P-adjusted net debt/EBITDA was ~2.2x at H1 FY26 within a 2-3x target range, but management itself expects gearing to drift toward ~2.6x by 2030 as growth capex (H1 FY26 alone: ~$208m growth + $64m stay-in-business) continues; a credit-rating downgrade from BBB+ would raise funding costs.

Unrealised mark-to-market moves on unhedged financial instruments (electricity swaps/options, carbon units) create large swings between EBITDAF and statutory NPAT — FY25 NPAT collapsed to just $1m (from $290m FY24) largely due to a $290m negative fair-value swing, and H1 FY25 was a $67m statutory loss despite decent underlying trading — this makes headline NPAT a poor guide to underlying performance and can spook less sophisticated investors.

financial.risk: Dividend vs. free cash flow gap
financial.description: With growth capex running well ahead of operating cash flow generation during the multi-year build programme, the 70-85% of free-cash-flow payout policy could mechanically compress free cash flow available for reinvestment, requiring more debt funding or dividend reinvestment plan (DRP) issuance (already used in FY25/H1 FY26) to bridge the gap, which is mildly dilutive.

regulatory.description: Following the Energy Competition Task Force review, the Electricity Authority has moved to require the four big gentailers (Mercury, Contact, Genesis, Meridian) to offer independent retailers the same wholesale/hedge terms they offer their own retail arms from around mid-2026/1 July 2026, alongside mandatory minimum hedge-trading volumes and a review of futures market-making. This directly targets the vertical-integration advantage that is part of Mercury's moat and could compress wholesale trading margins over time.

Business groups, some commentators and the OECD have publicly called for full operational (or even ownership) separation of generation from retail across the big four gentailers, citing NZ electricity market structure as a drag on productivity and competition. This remains on the table even though the Authority's initial package stopped short of forced separation — a change of political mood (especially given cost-of-living pressure) could escalate this.

As a 51%-Crown-owned company operating in a politically sensitive sector amid affordability concerns and post-winter-2024-shortage scrutiny, Mercury faces recurring risk of government intervention (price caps, windfall taxes, mandated market rule changes) that a purely private generator would not face to the same degree.

Dam safety regulations (new rules implemented in 2025), resource consent renewals for hydro/geothermal, and Fast Track Approvals Act processes all carry timing and conditionality risk for both existing assets and the development pipeline.

macro.description: As a highly capital-intensive, debt-funded utility with a large multi-year capex programme, Mercury's funding costs and the relative attractiveness of its dividend yield versus term deposits/bonds are both sensitive to NZ interest rate moves.

NZ's declining domestic gas production (management flags 'gas supply not meeting expectations') increases reliance on the wider system's thermal firming (e.g., Huntly, Genesis's coal/gas plant, the strategic energy reserve) during dry/low-wind periods, which indirectly drives the spot-price spikes that hurt Mercury's retail book even though Mercury itself burns no fossil fuel.

Mercury holds and actively trades New Zealand Units (NZUs) for trading purposes; the fair-value line on these carbon units is a real, if secondary, source of period-to-period earnings volatility (e.g., a $25m negative fair-value change on carbon units in H1 FY26) tied to the NZ ETS carbon price.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand needs a large wave of new renewable generation — management cites an estimated NZ$10 billion of new generation investment industry-wide through to 2030 with >4TWh of new renewables to be commissioned by 2027 — driven by electrification of transport/industry, the end of Tiwai Point aluminium smelter closure uncertainty (now extended), and retirement/uncertainty around thermal peaking capacity. NZ ranks in the World Energy Council's top ten Energy Trilemma Index but faces real near-term tension between security of supply, affordability and the pace of the renewables transition.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low economic-cycle sensitivity (electricity demand is largely non-discretionary) but high hydrological/weather cyclicality — wet vs. dry years materially swing generation volume, wholesale prices and reported earnings independent of the economic cycle.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — large, growing debt balance to fund the capex programme, and as a yield-oriented equity its relative valuation competes directly with term deposit/bond rates.
key_input_costs: Construction/EPC costs for wind and geothermal builds
Gas prices (indirectly, via system-wide thermal firming and spot price formation)
Carbon (NZU) prices under the NZ ETS
Skilled labour and turbine/generation equipment supply chains

recent_developments.event: FY2025 annual result: EBITDAF $786m (down $91m YoY, missed initial guidance) on generation volume of 7,906 GWh (down 10% YoY) driven by the 4th-lowest Waikato hydro year since 1980 (12th percentile inflows); statutory NPAT collapsed to just $1m (down $289m YoY) largely on a ~$290m negative fair-value swing on unhedged derivatives; full-year ordinary dividend 24.0 cps, up 3% (17th consecutive year of growth); FY26 EBITDAF guidance set at $1.0 billion and FY26 dividend guidance of 25.0 cps.

Stew Hamilton formally began as CEO (having stepped into the role from late August 2025), succeeding prior leadership; Board committee restructure (new Audit and Financial Risk Committee, Safety and Enterprise Risk Committee) effective 1 January 2025; several director departures/refreshes (Rob Hamilton joined the Board in April 2025; Lorraine Witten, James Miller and Mike Taitoko departing).

New Zealand electricity sector faced continued scrutiny after the winter 2024 supply-tightness/high-spot-price episode; Electricity Authority progressed its Energy Competition Task Force review, ultimately announcing 'level playing field' interventions (mandatory non-discrimination between independent and in-house retailers on hedge terms, minimum hedge-trading volume requirements, futures market-making review) targeted for implementation around mid-2026/1 July 2026, applying to Mercury, Contact, Genesis and Meridian.

Ngā Tamariki Geothermal Station's fifth generation unit (OEC5), a $220m expansion, was powered up in January 2026 and officially opened around March 2026, lifting station capacity from 86MW to 132MW and adding ~390GWh/yr of renewable baseload ahead of winter 2026.

H1 FY2026 interim result: EBITDAF $537m, up 28% on H1 FY25, on above-average hydro inflows; statutory NPAT $20m (vs. a $67m loss in H1 FY25); interim dividend 10.0 cps (up 4%); FY26 full-year guidance reiterated unchanged (EBITDAF $1.0bn, opex $370m, stay-in-business capex $150m, dividend 25.0 cps); net debt $2.243bn with S&P-adjusted net debt/EBITDA of ~2.2x, within the 2-3x target range; roughly half of H1 earnings (~$270m) reinvested into growth and existing generation assets; all three major builds (Ngā Tamariki OEC5, Kaiwera Downs II, Kaiwaikawe) tracking to schedule and budget.

FY2026 full-year result (year ended 30 June 2026) has NOT yet been released as of 13 August 2026; based on the FY25 reporting date (19 Aug), the FY26 result is expected in the second half of August 2026 and will be the next major catalyst, confirming whether the $1.0bn EBITDAF and 25.0 cps dividend guidance was met.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 result, 24 February 2026 (reiterating FY2025 result guidance from 19 August 2025)
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (year ended 30 June 2026) and FY2030 medium-term targets

items.notes: Reiterated unchanged at H1 FY26 (24 Feb 2026); H1 FY26 actual EBITDAF of $537m (up 28% YoY) tracking well against this target given above-average hydro inflows in the first half; original FY25 EBITDAF guidance was missed ($786m actual).
Would mark the 18th consecutive year of ordinary dividend increases if delivered; interim dividend of 10.0 cps (up 4%) already paid/declared at H1 FY26, consistent with full-year guidance track.
Part of the 'Core optimisation' key result under the FY30 strategic framework; H1 FY26 opex tracking below this run-rate per management commentary.
H1 FY26 actual was $64m; separate from growth capex which is running materially higher (~$208m in H1 FY26 alone, ~$347m for all of FY25).

items.vs_prior: new (introduced with refreshed FY35 strategic framework in FY25 annual report)
items.notes: Medium-term 'Key Result' under the 'Earnings transformation' strategic objective; implies EBITDAF growth of roughly 15-25% above FY26 guidance over four years.
Would represent roughly a 44% increase versus FY25 total generation of 7,906 GWh if fully delivered; supported by a development pipeline targeted to exceed 8TWh by 2030.

H1 FY26 actual was ~2.2x; management has flagged gearing will rise toward the upper-middle of the target range as the capex programme continues, which is consistent with the BBB+/Stable S&P rating being maintained rather than upgraded.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Stew Hamilton (in role since 31 August 2025) has framed FY26 as delivering on three simultaneous major builds (Ngā Tamariki OEC5, Kaiwera Downs II, Kaiwaikawe) representing ~$1bn of investment and 1.1TWh of new generation, while pursuing 'rebuilding confidence' in the sector after the winter 2024 supply-tightness episode damaged public and regulatory trust in gentailers. Guidance is explicitly caveated as subject to 'any material events, significant one-off expenses or other unforeseen circumstances including changes to hydrological conditions' — hydrology remains management's own primary flagged swing factor on guidance delivery. Chair Scott St John has emphasised the dividend policy target of 70-85% of free cash flow paid out on average over time, and has been vocal in defending gentailer market structure while calling for sector-wide firming solutions (maintaining thermal generation, improved gas information, investment signals for new firming) rather than forced structural separation.

dividend_profile.current_annual_dividend_guidance: 25.0 cps (FY2026 guidance), following 24.0 cps actual in FY2025
dividend_profile.track_record: 17 consecutive years of ordinary dividend growth through FY2025; would be 18 consecutive years if FY2026 guidance is delivered
dividend_profile.policy: Targets a payout of 70-85% of free cash flow on average over time (not a fixed percentage of NPAT, reflecting the fact that statutory NPAT is distorted by non-cash derivative/fair-value movements)
dividend_profile.approx_yield_context: At a share price around NZ$6.87-7.20 (August 2026), a 25.0 cps guided dividend implies a gross yield of roughly 3.5-3.6% before imputation credits (which are meaningful for NZ resident taxpayers given Mercury's dividends are typically fully imputed) — this is a lower headline yield than some domestic utility peers, reflecting the growth-capex/rerating premium the market has assigned to Mercury's development pipeline; the dividend is explicitly funded from a payout ratio of free cash flow rather than being fixed, so a persistently heavy capex cycle or a bad hydrology year could in principle pressure the pace of future increases even though management has so far protected the progressive track record via DRP issuance and gearing flexibility.

bull_case: Long, high-visibility renewable development pipeline (>8TWh by 2030, 3.5TWh new generation targeted) in a market structurally short of generation, with three major projects already tracking to schedule/budget and OEC5 geothermal freshly commissioned
FY30 EBITDAF target of $1.15-1.25bn implies meaningful earnings growth from FY26's $1.0bn guided base as the build programme lands, without needing further M&A

100% renewable, partially baseload (geothermal) generation mix is structurally advantaged versus thermal-exposed peers (e.g. Genesis) as NZ and global capital continues to reward decarbonised generation and electrification demand grows

18-year (if FY26 delivered) unbroken progressive dividend track record with a BBB+/Stable credit rating gives income-oriented investors a relatively predictable, imputed yield stream, underpinned by Crown ownership stability

H1 FY26 result shows the earnings recovery case playing out in real time — EBITDAF up 28% on a swing back to above-average hydrology, illustrating the operating leverage to a normal-to-wet year after two dry years suppressed FY24/FY25
bear_case: Hydrology is genuinely uncontrollable and has now produced two consecutive weak years (FY24, FY25) — a third dry year, or simply reversion after the strong H1 FY26 wet start, would again compress both volume and margin, and investors cannot reliably underwrite 'normalised' earnings from a business this weather-exposed

Regulatory risk is live and moving in a direction adverse to Mercury's economics: the Electricity Authority's 'level playing field' rules taking effect around mid-2026 are specifically designed to erode the wholesale-margin advantage gentailers extract from vertical integration, and calls for full generation-retail structural separation have not gone away — a re-escalation under political/affordability pressure is a real tail risk to the business model itself, not just to near-term earnings

The capex programme is large and multi-year, pushing gearing from ~2.2x toward management's own ~2.6x guided level by 2030 even before any project overrun, cost inflation, or execution slip across three simultaneous builds — any one of construction delay, dam-safety/consent friction, or supply-chain cost inflation could compress free cash flow available for the dividend precisely when the payout policy is explicitly tied to free cash flow rather than earnings

Statutory NPAT is extremely volatile and low-quality (essentially $0-1m in FY25 versus $290m the year before) due to large non-cash derivative and carbon fair-value swings, making conventional P/E-based valuation unreliable and requiring investors to trust management's EBITDAF/FCF framing rather than GAAP profit

51% Crown ownership is double-edged: it lends funding stability but structurally caps free float, limits capital-raising and takeover optionality (no other holder may exceed 10%), and exposes the stock to political risk — a government facing public anger over power prices has both the incentive and the 51% control to force pricing, market-rule or dividend-policy outcomes that would not be in minority shareholders' economic interest

The share currently trades near or above most published analyst price targets (~NZ$6.87-7.20 spot versus ~NZ$7.14-7.39 consensus target), leaving a thin margin of safety for a business whose next major data point (the FY2026 full-year result, expected mid-to-late August 2026) is still unreleased and could disappoint given the guidance caveat management itself attaches to hydrological conditions
